title: Database Systems
description: Databases as the heart of business applications. The course objectives: what a DBMS is and why it beats files; the relational vocabulary (tables, records, fields, primary and foreign keys, relations); designing a logical model and mapping it to a physical database; normalization to 1NF, 2NF and 3NF; SQL; and building a desktop application on top of a database. Taught by Saira Shaheen with section BS(CS)-4A. No week-by-week outline yet, so only the weeks with lectures in hand are listed. Marks: 4 quizzes × 3.5, 4 assignments × 4, midterm 30, final 40.
textbook: Elmasri & Navathe, Fundamentals of Database Systems (the lecture follows its chapter 1 closely). Connolly & Begg, Database Systems, and Hoffer, Modern Database Management, as secondary books.

modules.title: Why databases: the DBMS, the database approach, and who uses it
modules.outline: Lecture 1. Data, database, DBMS and database system. File processing versus the database approach. The characteristics of the database approach: self-description, data independence, multiple views, concurrency and ACID transactions, integrity, backup and recovery. When not to use a DBMS. Actors on the scene and the advantages of the DBMS approach.

lessons.title: From department files to one database
lessons.objective: define data, database, DBMS and database system in the textbook's words, and explain with an example why file processing leads to redundancy and inconsistency.

lessons.title: What makes the database approach different
lessons.objective: explain self-description, logical and physical data independence, multiple views and ACID transactions, classify a change as logical or physical, and say when a DBMS is the wrong tool.

lessons.title: Who uses a database, and what the DBMS buys you
lessons.objective: classify any person who touches a database into Elmasri's categories and list the advantages of the DBMS approach with a concrete feature for each.

lessons.title: Week 1 checkpoint
lessons.objective: answer the lecture's scenario questions and the week's definitions without notes.

modules.title: Data models, schemas and DBMS architectures
modules.outline: Lecture 2 (Elmasri chapter 2). Categories of data models (conceptual, representational, physical) and the four types the lecture names (relational, ER, object-oriented, semi-structured). Schema (intension) versus database state (extension, instance), schema constructs and schema evolution. The three-schema architecture revisited with the lecture's employee example. DDL, DML and SQL. DBMS component modules. Centralized, two-tier and three-tier client/server architectures.

lessons.title: Data models, schemas and database states
lessons.objective: classify a data model as conceptual, representational or physical, and tell a schema from a database state in any example.

lessons.title: DBMS languages and client/server architectures
lessons.objective: classify a statement as DDL or DML, name the DBMS component modules, and compare centralized, two-tier and three-tier architectures with a scenario.

modules.title: The Entity-Relationship model
modules.outline: Lecture 3 (Elmasri chapter 3). The database design process and where conceptual modelling fits. Chen's ER notation: entity types, entity sets and instances, strong and weak entities; simple, composite, single-valued, multivalued, stored, derived, NULL and complex attributes; relationships and cardinality ratios (1:1, 1:N, M:N) with participation. Keys: super, candidate, primary, alternate, foreign, composite. The car-sales case study. Quiz 1 on Friday 2 October covers lectures 01 to 03.

lessons.title: Entities and attributes in Chen notation
lessons.objective: draw any entity with its attributes in Chen notation and classify every attribute as simple or composite, single or multivalued, stored or derived.

lessons.title: Relationships, cardinality and keys
lessons.objective: read and write 1:1, 1:N and M:N relationships with participation, and list the super, candidate, primary and alternate keys of a table.

lessons.title: ERD lab: the car-sales case study
lessons.objective: turn a requirements paragraph into a complete Chen ER diagram: entities, attributes, keys, relationships and cardinalities.

lessons.title: Quiz 1 revision
lessons.objective: drill lectures 01 to 03 in quiz format before quiz 1 on Friday 2 October: definitions, schema levels, attribute and key types, and an ERD from a scenario.
